final_proof:
**Conventions and reading of the statement.** The statement contains evident typographical slips, which we correct in the only type-consistent way (this does not change the claim): the opposite functor of $L:\mathbf D\to\mathbf C$ is $L^{\text{op}}:\mathbf D^{\text{op}}\to\mathbf C^{\text{op}}$ (the displayed definition, written with $F$ and $\mathbf C$, is the general definition of the opposite functor, here applied to $F=L$), and the hom bifunctor of $\mathbf C$ is $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(-,-):\mathbf C^{\text{op}}\times\mathbf C\to\mathbf{Set}$. With these, $L^{\text{op}}\times\operatorname{id}_{\mathbf C}:\mathbf D^{\text{op}}\times\mathbf C\to\mathbf C^{\text{op}}\times\mathbf C$, so the composite $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(-,-)\circ(L^{\text{op}}\times\operatorname{id}_{\mathbf C})$ is a functor $\mathbf D^{\text{op}}\times\mathbf C\to\mathbf{Set}$, which has the same domain and codomain as $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(L-,-)$.

For a morphism $g:X\to Y$ of a category $\mathbf A$ we write $g^{\text{op}}:Y\to X$ for the corresponding morphism of $\mathbf A^{\text{op}}$; composition in $\mathbf A^{\text{op}}$ is $g^{\text{op}}\circ k^{\text{op}}=(k\circ g)^{\text{op}}$. Objects of $\mathbf A^{\text{op}}$ are those of $\mathbf A$. A morphism $(D,C)\to(D',C')$ in $\mathbf D^{\text{op}}\times\mathbf C$ is a pair $(g^{\text{op}},h)$ with $g:D'\to D$ in $\mathbf D$ and $h:C\to C'$ in $\mathbf C$.

**Definitions used.**

1. *Hom bifunctor.* Since $\mathbf C$ is locally small, each $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(X,C)$ is a set. $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(-,-):\mathbf C^{\text{op}}\times\mathbf C\to\mathbf{Set}$ sends an object $(X,C)$ to $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(X,C)$, and a morphism $(f^{\text{op}},h):(X,C)\to(X',C')$ (so $f:X'\to X$, $h:C\to C'$) to the mapping
$$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(f,h):\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(X,C)\to\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(X',C'),\qquad \varphi\mapsto h\circ\varphi\circ f .$$

2. *Hom bifunctor with left functor.* $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(L-,-):\mathbf D^{\text{op}}\times\mathbf C\to\mathbf{Set}$ sends an object $(D,C)$ to $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(LD,C)$, and a morphism $(g^{\text{op}},h):(D,C)\to(D',C')$ (so $g:D'\to D$, $h:C\to C'$) to the mapping
$$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(Lg,h):\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(LD,C)\to\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(LD',C'),\qquad \varphi\mapsto h\circ\varphi\circ Lg .$$
(This is well typed: $Lg:LD'\to LD$, $\varphi:LD\to C$, $h:C\to C'$.)

3. *Opposite functor.* $L^{\text{op}}:\mathbf D^{\text{op}}\to\mathbf C^{\text{op}}$ sends an object $D$ to $LD$ and a morphism $g^{\text{op}}$ to $(Lg)^{\text{op}}$. It is a functor: $L^{\text{op}}(\mathrm{id}_D)=(L\,\mathrm{id}_D)^{\text{op}}=\mathrm{id}_{LD}$, and $L^{\text{op}}(g^{\text{op}}\circ k^{\text{op}})=L^{\text{op}}((k\circ g)^{\text{op}})=(Lk\circ Lg)^{\text{op}}=(Lg)^{\text{op}}\circ(Lk)^{\text{op}}=L^{\text{op}}(g^{\text{op}})\circ L^{\text{op}}(k^{\text{op}})$.

4. *Product of functors.* For $F:\mathbf A\to\mathbf A'$ and $G:\mathbf B\to\mathbf B'$, $F\times G:\mathbf A\times\mathbf B\to\mathbf A'\times\mathbf B'$ acts componentwise: $(A,B)\mapsto(FA,GB)$ and $(a,b)\mapsto(Fa,Gb)$. Hence $L^{\text{op}}\times\operatorname{id}_{\mathbf C}$ sends $(D,C)\mapsto(LD,C)$ and $(g^{\text{op}},h)\mapsto((Lg)^{\text{op}},h)$.

5. *Composite functor.* For $F:\mathbf A\to\mathbf B$, $G:\mathbf B\to\mathbf E$, $G\circ F$ sends each object $A$ to $G(FA)$ and each morphism $a$ to $G(Fa)$.

6. *Equality of functors.* A functor between two given categories consists exactly of its object mapping and its morphism mapping; two functors $\mathbf A\to\mathbf B$ are equal precisely when these two mappings coincide, i.e. they agree on every object and on every morphism.

**Proof.** Put $H:=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(-,-)\circ(L^{\text{op}}\times\operatorname{id}_{\mathbf C})$. Both $H$ and $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(L-,-)$ are functors $\mathbf D^{\text{op}}\times\mathbf C\to\mathbf{Set}$, so by (6) it suffices to show that they agree on objects and on morphisms.

*Objects.* Let $(D,C)$ be an object of $\mathbf D^{\text{op}}\times\mathbf C$. By (5), (4) and (1),
$$H(D,C)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(-,-)\big((L^{\text{op}}\times\operatorname{id}_{\mathbf C})(D,C)\big)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(-,-)(LD,C)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(LD,C),$$
which by (2) is $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(L-,-)(D,C)$.

*Morphisms.* Let $(g^{\text{op}},h):(D,C)\to(D',C')$ be a morphism of $\mathbf D^{\text{op}}\times\mathbf C$, with $g:D'\to D$ in $\mathbf D$ and $h:C\to C'$ in $\mathbf C$. By (5) and (4),
$$H(g^{\text{op}},h)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(-,-)\big((Lg)^{\text{op}},h\big).$$
Here $((Lg)^{\text{op}},h):(LD,C)\to(LD',C')$ is a morphism of $\mathbf C^{\text{op}}\times\mathbf C$ with $Lg:LD'\to LD$ in $\mathbf C$, so by (1), applied with $X=LD$, $X'=LD'$, $f=Lg$, it is the mapping
$$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(LD,C)\to\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(LD',C'),\qquad \varphi\mapsto h\circ\varphi\circ Lg .$$
By (2) this is exactly $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(L-,-)(g^{\text{op}},h)$: the two mappings have the same domain $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(LD,C)$, the same codomain $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(LD',C')$, and the same value $h\circ\varphi\circ Lg$ at every $\varphi$.

Since $H$ and $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(L-,-)$ have the same domain and codomain and agree on all objects and all morphisms, they are equal:
$$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(L-,-)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(-,-)\circ\big(L^{\text{op}}\times\operatorname{id}_{\mathbf C}\big).\qquad\blacksquare$$

*Remark.* The equality is a strict equality (not merely a natural isomorphism) because $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(L-,-)$ is *defined* by the object and morphism assignments in (2), which the computation above shows coincide literally with those of the composite; no independent choice (e.g. of a representing object) is involved.
